First off, this is unlikely to occur in the "nightmare" scenario a few of you are thinking wherein Microsoft would try to take over all PC gaming and levy a toll to play online. The main reason this could not happen is that as long as there is competition on Windows (e.g. Steam and GoG), it would never fly. Such a scenario is more likely on SteamOS where Valve/Steam have completel control and no competition. In fact, you can make a strong argument that Steam has a virtual monopoly on PC gaming already, and this has resulted in much anti-gamer behavior on their part since physical media has all but disappeared and left gamers with no viable alternative.

But back to Microsoft and XBox Live. I'm a PC gamer, but I own an XBox One for the media features. I pay about $40 a year for XBox Live (by waiting for a sale). I don't need it, but it gets me 4 free games a month (two native XBox One games, and two 360 games I can play on XBox One). So I get 48 games a year for $40. By any measure, that's a tremendous value. I can stream those games to my PC and play them there if I like. And Major Nelson has already stated that they'll be adding keyboard & mouse support to gaming on the XBox One--and all of that is happening within Microsoft's XBox "walled garden" with no internal competition.

So if they offer a similar service on the PC where they (currently) do have competition? I'll have to wait and see....but if it's as good a value as what they offer on the XBox One, I'll absolutely consider it. The take-away from all of this is two-fold. First, Microsoft is actually interested in giving gamers value for their money. Second, gamers benefit when there is competition on Windows; as long as that exists it will be impossible for one company to treat gamers poorly without severe repercussions to their bottom line.

Give us a little more background on you? I mean, I'm a Wyoming (USA state, least populated, lots of empty land) native, camping started out as simply staying near an activity you wanted to do. Hiking in Yellowstone, fishing one of the dozens of high altitude lakes, attending a Rendezvous, throw up a tent/tepee to save yourself hours (and hours) of driving.

As I got older, I continued with the same principle, I'd camp out at racetracks because it was free and I didn't want to spend hours trying to commute. I'd camp on roadtrips because it was free (ninja camping, FTW) and I wanted to do some exploring. But the more you do it, the more you Experience things. For instance, I was doing some unpaved exploring in Colorado and wound up camping in dinosaur national monument for the night. You're surrounded by 1,000 tall cliffs on all sides, and a thunderstorm rolled through. The experience is easily a top 5 in my life, probably a top 3... the sound, the light (no rain, little wind, just cloud to cloud lightning), it was just phenomenal.

So now I Also camp for experiences... this last Super Moon I camped out on a lake to take in the full experience with as little light pollution and as big a view as possible. I still camp for a simple place to stay (sandbar on a river on a multi-night kayak trip, as well as the nights before and after as I'm usually more than a days drive from home), but it's not the only reason.

If you don't do outdoor activities though, I can see how it's confusing. You get hot and sticky when it's hot, wet when it rains, cold when it's cold out, have to find a way to clean yourself occasionally, carry food/water, own/have access to specialized equipment... it can be miserable, even for people who Like to do it. And it's not for everyone...

But what do YOU do for fun? Do you live in a city? (Gah, kill me first ~ I can deal with about 3~4 days of being somewhere with a pop greater than 10k people, then I'm looking for a bell tower and a scoped rifle). Do you spend money on going to the movies? (I haven't in nearly 2 decades and don't understand why anyone wastes their money these days). The point I'm trying to make is that you do something that comes across as a mundane, worthless and useless activity to others. Yet, you derive joy from it and continue to do that activity despite costs/difficult access/personal inconvenience. It's a life experience you find enjoyable, and that's camping for a lot of people.

When I'm hiking, or even when I'm car camping, virtually everything I do is done with purpose. If I don't keep walking, I won't make it to where I planned to have lunch. There's none of the daily bullshit of modern life. I'm not trapped in concrete, wood and steel. I can breathe clean air and swim in crystaline waters. I can wake to the sound of birds, and hear the yip of coyotes in the night. I can hang a hammock between two trees and nap in the sun, or read a good book.
